fields.sample_size: ethnographic study in Gulu, Mbarara and Kampala (Uganda): 18 focus group discussions with 126 participants plus interviews, community meetings and observation; inductive and deductive thematic analysis
fields.effect_estimate: Poor slum sanitation, worst in Kampala, is driven by urban migration to escape rural poverty, urban governance deficits and corruption, the survival imperative, poor service delivery and lack of capacity to plan and enforce, pervasive informality, absence of enforced standards ('to whom it may concern' attitudes) and normalisation of risk; sanitation choices are shared on-site facilities (up to 30 people or 7 households per facility). The authors argue sanitation cannot be solved by single interventions and must be nested within reframing of urbanisation. Qualitative.
fields.study_design: ethnographic multi-site qualitative study (focus groups, interviews, observation) in three urban centres
fields.section: Full text: Methods (design, 18 FGDs with 126 participants, community meetings); Results (demand, supply, access, use, sustainability); Conclusions
fields.exact_location: Methods (design, 18 FGDs with 126 participants, community meetings); Results (demand, supply, access, use, sustainability); Conclusions

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: an ethnographic study of urban slum sanitation in Gulu, Mbarara and Kampala (18 focus groups, 126 participants), read in full text 2026-10-04. Governance deficits, corruption, lack of enforced standards and informality sustain poor sanitation; economic survival outranks sanitation standards.
